deepDive.title: Asexual vs sexual — when and why each strategy wins
deepDive.body: Class 7 introduces both reproduction modes. Class 8 explores the trade-offs. ASEXUAL: fast (no partner needed), cheap (no flowers/gametes to make), and OFFSPRING ARE CLONES — identical to parent. Great when conditions are favourable + stable. Risk: a disease that kills one kills ALL (Cavendish banana clone vulnerability). SEXUAL: slow, expensive (flowers, nectar to attract pollinators), and OFFSPRING ARE GENETICALLY MIXED — different from parents. Great when conditions are changing or pathogens are common — variation gives some offspring resistance. Most plants do BOTH — sexual in good times for variation, asexual in stress for rapid colonisation. Strawberries: produce both seeds AND runners. Indian agriculture exploits this — propagate desired cultivars asexually for predictability, breed new ones sexually for variation.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 10 covers Mendel's experiments — sexual reproduction's genetic mathematics.

deepDive.title: Mendel's laws — peas, ratios, and the birth of genetics
deepDive.body: Class 7 says sexual reproduction mixes parental traits. Class 10 reveals the MATH behind it. Gregor Mendel (1865, Austrian monk) bred pea plants — short × tall, yellow × green seeds — and noted exact RATIOS in offspring. His laws: (1) LAW OF SEGREGATION: each parent contributes one 'factor' (gene) per trait; the pair segregates in gametes. (2) LAW OF INDEPENDENT ASSORTMENT: different traits inherit independently (height doesn't drag along seed colour). (3) Dominance: in heterozygous offspring, one allele MASKS the other. The famous 3:1 ratio (tall : short in F2 generation) emerges from these. Mendel's work was ignored for 35 years, then rediscovered around 1900 — the foundation of all modern genetics. Indian Green Revolution wheat varieties were bred using Mendelian principles + statistics.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle after Class 8 sexual vs asexual.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11/12 expands Mendelian to Mendelian + chromosomal + molecular genetics.

deepDive.title: Double fertilisation — the unique flowering plant trick
deepDive.body: Class 7 says pollen fertilises egg → seed. Class 11 reveals flowering plants do TWO simultaneous fertilisations — unique in nature. Pollen tube delivers TWO male gametes. ONE fuses with the egg → makes the embryo (the actual baby plant). The OTHER fuses with TWO POLAR NUCLEI → makes the ENDOSPERM (food storage tissue in the seed). The endosperm is what you EAT in rice, wheat, maize — it's mostly endosperm! This DOUBLE FERTILISATION evolved ~130 million years ago, when flowering plants exploded across Earth. It's incredibly efficient: no resources wasted on endosperm if fertilisation fails. Only flowering plants (angiosperms) do this. Pine trees + ferns don't.
deepDive.nextStepHint: NEET tests the embryo sac structure (7 cells, 8 nuclei) — site of double fertilisation.
